etymology: The Second London Baptist Confession of Faith, drafted in 1677 under persecution and published openly in 1689 after the Act of Toleration; the confessional standard of the Particular (Reformed) Baptists — and of this dictionary.
biblical_def: The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith is the mature doctrinal standard of the Particular Baptists, and the confessional standard against which this dictionary is audited. Drafted in 1677, when open publication invited prison, and issued publicly in 1689 once toleration came, it deliberately followed the Westminster Confession and the Savoy Declaration wherever it could — to show the world that Baptists stood squarely within the Reformed faith — while amending what Scripture required: the church as a congregation of visible saints, baptism as the immersion of professing believers, and the independence of each local congregation under Christ. Its thirty-two chapters confess the Scriptures as the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule; God's sovereign decree; the covenant of grace; Christ the Mediator; effectual calling, justification, adoption, sanctification, and the perseverance of the saints; the moral law's abiding rule; gospel worship and the Lord's day; and the last judgment. Men like William Kiffin, Hanserd Knollys, and Benjamin Keach set their names to it, and Nehemiah Coxe likely edited it. The confession does not rival Scripture but serves it — a public, accountable summary of what the Scriptures teach, holding fast the form of sound words (2 Tim 1:13) so that churches and generations may know, test, and keep the faith once delivered to the saints.

corruption_summary: The confession is corrupted from two directions: a 'no creed but the Bible' biblicism that leaves every man his own theologian and the church defenseless against error, and a dead confessionalism that recites the document without believing or obeying it.
corruption_paragraphs: No-creed biblicism. The modern evangelical slogan 'no creed but Christ' sounds humble but works mischief: a church that refuses to say publicly WHAT it believes the Bible teaches cannot test its teachers, guard its members, or hand the faith intact to its children — every wind of doctrine blows through unhindered. The dictionary holds the confessional principle: Scripture alone is the infallible rule, and precisely BECAUSE it is, the church must publicly confess its sense of Scripture in a form that can be examined, challenged from the text, and held to account. The 1689 binds no conscience above the Word; it binds teachers to say plainly what they take the Word to mean.

Dead-confessionalism correction. The opposite corruption subscribes the confession as a heritage badge while the pulpit and the life drift from it. The men of 1689 signed at the risk of prison; their confession was a living testimony, not a museum piece. The dictionary holds that confessional subscription is a solemn promise before God — the document is to be taught, preached, believed, and obeyed, and where a man can no longer hold it he must say so honestly rather than hollow it out from within.

etymology: The briefer of the two catechisms produced by the Westminster Assembly (1647), designed to teach the faith to children and new believers by question and answer.
biblical_def: The Westminster Shorter Catechism is the briefer of the two catechisms framed by the Westminster Assembly in 1647, written so that children and those 'of weaker capacity' might learn the substance of the Christian faith by plain question and answer. Its opening question is among the most celebrated sentences outside Scripture: 'What is the chief end of man? Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.' In one hundred seven questions it walks the learner through what man is to believe concerning God — the Scriptures, God's nature and decrees, creation, providence, the fall, Christ the Redeemer in His offices and states, and the application of redemption — and what duty God requires of man: the Ten Commandments opened one by one, faith and repentance, the Word, the sacraments, and the Lord's Prayer petition by petition. Its definitions ('Justification is an act of God's free grace...'; 'Sanctification is the work of God's free grace...') have given generations their doctrinal vocabulary. The Baptists so valued it that their own Baptist Catechism (1693) reproduces it nearly entire, amended on baptism. It stands in the dictionary as the master tool of catechesis — the deliberate, ordered teaching of sound words to the next generation, that the children of the church might know whom they have believed.

corruption_summary: The catechism is corrupted when catechesis itself is abandoned — dismissed as rote 'indoctrination' and replaced with entertainment — leaving a generation that cannot say what it believes or why.
corruption_paragraphs: Indoctrination-smear correction. The age calls it indoctrination to teach a child fixed answers about God, while cheerfully catechizing the same child in its own dogmas through every screen and classroom. The question is never WHETHER a child will be catechized but BY WHOM. The dictionary holds the biblical command: parents are to teach God's words diligently to their children, in the house and by the way (Deut 6:7); deliberate, ordered instruction in the truth is not the violation of a child's mind but the feeding of it.

Entertainment-replacement correction. Much modern children's ministry trades doctrine for amusement, assuming young minds cannot bear definitions. The Shorter Catechism assumes the opposite and has proven it for nearly four centuries: children can carry 'God is a Spirit, infinite, eternal, and unchangeable' for life, and the definitions memorized young become the rails on which a lifetime of faith runs. The dictionary commends the recovery of catechesis — in the home and the church — as a first duty to the next generation.

etymology: The Davidic line that reigned in Jerusalem from the division of the kingdom (Rehoboam, c. 931 BC) to the Babylonian captivity (Zedekiah, 586 BC) — about twenty kings, every one a son of David.
biblical_def: The kings of Judah are the unbroken Davidic line that reigned in Jerusalem from Rehoboam, under whom the kingdom divided, to Zedekiah, under whom it fell to Babylon — roughly twenty kings across three and a half centuries, every one descended from David. Their record is deliberately mixed. Judah had true reformers the northern kingdom never had: Asa who removed the idols, Jehoshaphat who sent teachers of the law through the cities, Hezekiah who trusted the LORD 'so that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah' (2 Kgs 18:5), and Josiah who, on finding the book of the law, tore his clothes and purged the land. It also had apostates as dark as any in Israel: Ahaz who burned his children in the fire, and Manasseh who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood. Yet through good kings and monsters alike, one thread holds the account together: 'for David's sake did the LORD his God give him a lamp in Jerusalem' (1 Kgs 15:4). The dynasty was preserved not by the kings' merit but by God's covenant with David, until the line issued — through exile and obscurity — in 'Jesus Christ, the son of David' (Matt 1:1), the King whose throne is established for ever and of whose kingdom there shall be no end.

corruption_summary: The kings of Judah are corrupted when their history is read as mere ancient politics, missing the covenant thread — the dynasty preserved for David's sake until Christ — that makes the whole account gospel history.
corruption_paragraphs: Politics-only misreading. Secular treatment reads Judah's kings as one more Near-Eastern dynasty, its survival a fluke of geography. Scripture reads it as covenant: through twenty reigns, assassinations, Athaliah's massacre, and Babylon's furnace, the lamp of David never went out, because God had sworn that David's house and throne would be established for ever (2 Sam 7:16). The dictionary holds the line of Judah as the spine of redemptive history — every preserved heir a mile-marker on the road to the Messiah.

Beyond this, the entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honesty of the inspired record. Scripture does not whitewash David's house: the same chronicle that crowns Hezekiah and Josiah exposes Manasseh's blood and Zedekiah's faithlessness, and judgment fell on the covenant dynasty itself. The dictionary commends the lesson: God's promises do not exempt His people from His holiness, and the certainty of the covenant rests on the faithfulness of God, never on the virtue of men.

etymology: The Lord Jesus' great discourse in Matthew 5-7, delivered on a mountain in Galilee to His disciples in the hearing of the multitudes; the fullest single statement of the ethics of His kingdom.
biblical_def: The Sermon on the Mount is the Lord Jesus' great discourse in Matthew 5 through 7, the fullest single declaration of the character and conduct of the citizens of His kingdom. It opens with the Beatitudes, pronouncing blessing on the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, and the persecuted — a portrait of grace-wrought character, not a ladder of merit. The Lord then declares His relation to the law: 'Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil' (Matt 5:17), and in six antitheses drives the commandments beneath the surface to the heart — anger as murder's root, lust as adultery's seed — demanding a righteousness exceeding that of the scribes. He teaches secret giving, the Lord's Prayer, treasure in heaven, trust over anxiety, the narrow gate, and the test of fruits, and He closes with the two builders: 'whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them' builds on rock (Matt 7:24). The crowds were astonished, 'for he taught them as one having authority' (Matt 7:29). The sermon is neither a plan of salvation by works nor a beautiful impossibility: it is the law of the King for a people already His by grace, describing the life that flows from the new heart His Spirit gives.

corruption_summary: The Sermon is corrupted when it is cut loose from the cross and made a self-saving ethic or a merely social program, and equally when it is postponed to another age so that its commands no longer bind the church today.
corruption_paragraphs: Ethics-without-atonement misreading. Liberal religion has long treated the Sermon as the 'real' Christianity — a noble ethic that needs no atoning blood — as though men could climb the Beatitudes to heaven. The Sermon itself forbids this: it demands a righteousness exceeding the scribes', purity of heart, perfection as the Father is perfect — a standard that slays self-righteousness and drives the sinner to the Savior who fulfilled all righteousness and bled for those who had none. The dictionary holds that the Sermon describes the fruit of salvation, never its price; severed from the cross it is not good news but a death sentence.

Postponement misreading. The opposite error defers the Sermon to a future dispensation, as though its commands were not for the church now. But the Lord closed it by binding ALL hearers to do these sayings on pain of ruin (Matt 7:24-27), and commissioned His church to teach the nations 'to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.' The dictionary holds the Sermon as the present law of the King for His present people — kingdom ethics in force wherever the King reigns, until He comes.

etymology: From Greek protos (first) + euangelion (gospel): "the first gospel" — the church's ancient name for Genesis 3:15, the first promise of the Redeemer.
biblical_def: The protoevangelium ('first gospel') is the church's ancient name for Genesis 3:15, the first promise of redemption, spoken by God in the very hour of the fall — and spoken, remarkably, not to Adam but to the serpent, as a sentence of doom: 'And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.' Before any curse fell on the man or the woman, God promised a Champion. Three things are pledged. First, sovereign enmity: God Himself would break the fatal alliance between man and the devil, setting a war of the seeds in motion — the line of the woman against the offspring of the serpent, traced through all Scripture. Second, a wounded victory: the serpent would bruise the Champion's heel — a real, painful, but not final wound. Third, a crushed head: the seed of the woman would deal the destroying blow. The whole Bible unfolds from this seed-promise: 'when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman' (Gal 4:4), who at the cross was bruised in the heel and in that very bruising crushed the serpent's head, 'that he might destroy the works of the devil' (1 John 3:8). The gospel was preached first by God, in Eden, over the rubble of the fall.
webster_summary: Genesis 3:15, the 'first gospel': God's promise in the hour of the fall that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent's head while being bruised in the heel — fulfilled in Christ, born of a woman, destroying the devil's works at the cross.

corruption_summary: The protoevangelium is corrupted when critical scholarship flattens Genesis 3:15 into a primitive folk-tale about why men dislike snakes, denying the messianic promise that God Himself planted at the head of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Folk-tale flattening. The higher-critical reading calls Genesis 3:15 an etiology — an ancient just-so story explaining snake-loathing — and rules out any messianic sense as later Christian imagination. The text itself refuses the shrinkage: the enmity is set by God's own decree, the combatants are persons ('he... his heel'), and the rest of Scripture consciously takes up the thread — the seed promised to Abraham, narrowed to Judah and to David, until Paul declares the God of peace about to bruise Satan under the church's feet (Rom 16:20). The dictionary reads Genesis 3:15 as the Lord Jesus read Moses: as Scripture that speaks of Him.

Beyond the critical flattening, the entry calls for recovering a principle: grace announced before judgment was executed. God preached the gospel in Eden before He pronounced the curses and before He clothed the guilty pair — mercy had the first word over the ruin. The dictionary commends the comfort: from the first sin onward, God's posture toward His fallen people has been promise; the whole Bible is the outworking of a rescue declared in the moment the wound was made.

etymology: Three fourth-century theologians of Cappadocia (in modern Turkey): Basil of Caesarea, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus — chief defenders of the deity of the Son and the Spirit after Nicaea.
biblical_def: The Cappadocian Fathers are three fourth-century pastors and theologians from Cappadocia — Basil of Caesarea (called 'the Great'), his younger brother Gregory of Nyssa, and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus ('the Theologian') — whom God used to carry the Nicene confession of Christ's full deity through the generation of fierce Arian reaction after the council of Nicaea (325). When emperors and councils wavered and Arianism nearly captured the church, these men contended — against the Arians, who made the Son a creature, and the Eunomians, who claimed God's essence was fully comprehensible — that the Son is of one essence with the Father, and they extended the same confession to the Holy Spirit (Basil's treatise On the Holy Spirit defending the Spirit's deity and worship). Their careful language — one divine essence, three distinct persons — gave the church its grammar for confessing the Trinity, and bore fruit at the council of Constantinople (381), which reaffirmed and completed the Nicene Creed. The dictionary honors them, from a Reformed standpoint, as gifts of Christ to His church for the defense of truths the Scriptures plainly teach: that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the one God (Matt 28:19), and that he who has seen the Son has seen the Father.
webster_summary: Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory of Nazianzus — fourth-century defenders of the full deity of the Son and the Spirit against Arianism, whose Trinitarian language bore fruit at Constantinople (381).

corruption_summary: The Cappadocians are corrupted when the Trinity they defended is dismissed as Greek philosophy imposed on a simple Jesus, or when their honored memory is stretched to authorize later traditions Scripture nowhere teaches.
corruption_paragraphs: Hellenization-myth correction. A standard critical claim holds that the Nicene Trinity was Greek metaphysics smothering the simple religion of Jesus. The Cappadocians themselves refute it: their doctrine was forged in exegesis — the baptismal name (Matt 28:19), the Word who was God (John 1:1), the threefold benediction (2 Cor 13:14) — and their philosophical vocabulary was pressed into service OF the text, not over it. The dictionary holds that the Trinity is not a later accretion but the Bible's own teaching, defended with the church's best tools by men who bled for it.

Tradition-stretched caution. Because the Cappadocians stand so tall, later traditions claim their mantle for practices and doctrines — monastic merit, the veneration system, an infallible conciliar magisterium — that Scripture does not teach. The dictionary honors these fathers as the Reformers did: eminent servants whose witness to the Trinity we gladly receive BECAUSE it is scriptural, while testing all their words, like all men's words, by the Word. The fathers are weighty witnesses; Scripture alone is the rule.

etymology: The New Testament's revelation that believing Gentiles are made fellow heirs with believing Israel in the one people of God — promised to Abraham, opened at Cornelius's house, settled at the Jerusalem Council, and expounded in Ephesians 2-3 and Romans 9-11.
biblical_def: Gentile inclusion is the New Testament's glad announcement that in Christ the nations are brought into the one people of God on equal footing with believing Israel — not as guests, but as heirs. The promise was ancient: in Abraham's seed all families of the earth would be blessed. The Lord Jesus commanded discipleship of all nations, and the door swung open in the book of Acts: at Cornelius's house Peter confessed, 'Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons' (Acts 10:34), and the Jerusalem Council ruled that Gentile believers are saved by grace through faith without circumcision (Acts 15). Paul unfolds the mystery: Christ 'is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition' (Eph 2:14), creating of Jew and Gentile one new man, one body, one household built on the prophets and apostles. In Romans 11 the figure is an olive tree: wild branches grafted in among the natural, sharing the root's fatness — with a warning against Gentile boasting, and a promise that God has not cast away His ancient people. 'If ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise' (Gal 3:29). The church of Jew and Gentile together is not God's afterthought but the mystery hid from ages, now displayed to principalities and powers as His manifold wisdom.

corruption_summary: Gentile inclusion is corrupted when it is recast as mere modern 'inclusivity' — acceptance without repentance and faith — and when Gentile believers boast against the natural branches, forgetting the root bears them.
corruption_paragraphs: Inclusivity-without-faith misreading. The age borrows the Bible's welcome of the nations to preach a different doctrine: that God includes everyone as they are, no repentance required. Scripture's Gentile inclusion is nothing of the kind: Cornelius heard words whereby he must be SAVED; the council confessed that Gentiles' hearts were 'purified by faith'; the wild branches stand 'by faith' and are warned they too can be cut off. The dictionary holds that the door God opened to the nations is the door of the gospel — wide as the world, and entered only by repentance toward God and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.

Gentile-boasting correction. Paul's olive tree carries a warning the Gentile church has often trampled: 'Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee' (Rom 11:18). Contempt for the Jewish people inverts the whole figure — the church owes Israel the oracles, the covenants, the Christ. The dictionary holds with the apostle: no arrogance toward the natural branches, earnest desire for their salvation, and confidence that the Deliverer who came out of Zion has not finished with the people He foreknew.
roots_summary: The nations made fellow heirs in the one people of God — opened at Cornelius's house, settled at the Jerusalem Council, expounded as the one new man and the grafted olive branches.

etymology: From Greek anthropos (man) + logos (word, study): the Bible's doctrine of man — his creation in God's image, his constitution as body and soul, his fall, and his end.
biblical_def: Biblical anthropology is the Scripture's own doctrine of man: what he is, whence he came, what went wrong, and what he is for. Its foundation is creation: 'So God created man in his own image... male and female created he them' (Gen 1:27). Man is not an accident of matter but a creature made by God's deliberate counsel, formed of the dust and inbreathed with the breath of life so that he became a living soul (Gen 2:7) — a real body and a real soul in one person, crowned with glory and honor as God's image-bearer and given dominion under God. The image confers both dignity and accountability: every human life, from the womb to old age, bears God's stamp and is therefore sacred; and every human life answers to its Maker. Created male and female — equal in the image, distinct and complementary in calling — man was made good, fell in Adam into sin and death, and is now corrupted in every faculty: 'all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God' (Rom 3:23). Yet the image, defaced, is not erased; and in Christ, the true image of the invisible God, it is renewed in knowledge, righteousness, and holiness. Man's chief end is not self-definition or self-fulfillment but to glorify God and enjoy Him for ever.
webster_summary: The Bible's doctrine of man: created in God's image, body and soul, male and female, made good and fallen in Adam, every faculty corrupted yet the image not erased, renewed in Christ; man's end is to glorify God, not to define himself.

corruption_summary: Biblical anthropology is assaulted from two sides: a materialism that reduces man to an accidental animal or a machine, and an expressive individualism that makes the self its own creator, defining identity, purpose, and even male and female by inner feeling rather than the Maker's design.
corruption_paragraphs: Materialist reduction. The secular academy teaches that man is an unplanned animal — chemistry that learned to talk — with no soul, no image, and no end beyond survival. Scripture answers with Genesis 2:7: man is formed BY God and FOR God, body and soul, crowned with glory and honor (Psa 8:5). The dictionary holds the whole grandeur and the whole accountability together: because man bears the image, every life is sacred and no man is autonomous; the creature who came from God's hand answers to God's judgment.

Self-definition inversion. The reigning creed of the age — expressive individualism, with its gender ideology — teaches that the self is discovered within and constructed at will, so that even 'male and female' yield to inner feeling. Scripture locates identity in creation, not introspection: 'male and female created he them' is the Maker's gift, not the self's project, and the body is not raw material for self-invention but a stewardship from God. The dictionary holds the biblical order: man receives himself from God, loses himself in rebellion, and finds himself only in Christ, in whom the defaced image is renewed.
roots_summary: The Bible's doctrine of man: God's image-bearer, body and soul, male and female, fallen in Adam, renewed in Christ — received from the Maker, not defined by the self.

etymology: Latin versio vulgata, "the common version"; Jerome's Latin translation of the Scriptures (c. 382-405), made from the Hebrew and Greek, which became the Bible of the Western church for a thousand years.
biblical_def: The Vulgate is the Latin translation of the Scriptures executed chiefly by Jerome between about 382 and 405, which became the common Bible of the Western church for over a millennium. Commissioned to revise the chaotic Old Latin versions, Jerome did something more radical: for the Old Testament he went behind the Greek Septuagint to the Hebrew itself — his principle of Hebraica veritas, 'the Hebrew truth' — insisting that the church's translation stand on the original tongues. The result served Christendom for centuries and gave the West much of its theological vocabulary. Its later history, though, is a parable. What began as a translation INTO the common tongue (vulgata, 'common') hardened into a sacred barrier: as Latin died among the people, the common version became the closed book, and Rome at the Council of Trent declared this translation 'authentic,' practically setting it above the Hebrew and Greek from which Jerome himself had worked. The Reformers honored Jerome's labor and followed his principle — back to the originals, then forward into the tongues of the people — which is precisely the lineage of the English Bible and the King James Version. The dictionary holds the Vulgate in honor as a monumental work of believing scholarship, and holds its history as a standing lesson: translations serve the Word; they must never be enthroned over it.
webster_summary: Jerome's Latin Bible (c. 382-405), translated from the Hebrew and Greek ('Hebraica veritas'), the Western church's Bible for a millennium; begun as the common version, later wrongly enthroned by Trent above the original tongues it was drawn from.

corruption_summary: The Vulgate's story is corrupted when its lesson is missed: a translation made for the people became a relic locked against them, and a servant of the originals was enthroned above them — errors the Reformation overturned and every age must guard against.
corruption_paragraphs: Translation-enthroned correction. Trent's decree treating the Latin as the church's authentic standard inverted Jerome's own principle: he labored back to the Hebrew truth precisely because no translation, however venerable, outranks the inspired originals. The dictionary holds the Reformation's order, which is Jerome's order: the Hebrew and Greek Scriptures are the immediately inspired Word; translations — the Vulgate, the King James, all of them — are faithful servants to be tested by the fountainhead, never enthroned over it.

Closed-book correction. The 'common version' became, by the slow death of Latin, the locked version — the Scriptures chained in a tongue the plowboy could not read, until Wycliffe, Tyndale, and the Reformers gave the Word back to the people. The dictionary holds with Nehemiah 8:8 and 1 Corinthians 14:9: the Word of God is meant to be read distinctly, with the sense given, in words easy to be understood. The entrance of His words gives light to the simple (Psa 119:130) — and whatever obscures that entrance, however hallowed, must give way.

etymology: The second word of the Decalogue (Exo 20:4-6): the prohibition of graven images and of worship by means of them — governing not WHOM we worship (the first commandment) but HOW.
biblical_def: The second commandment is the second word of the Decalogue: 'Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image... thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God' (Exo 20:4-5). Where the first commandment fixes the OBJECT of worship — no other gods — the second governs its MANNER: the true God must not be worshiped by images or by any means of man's devising. Moses presses the ground of it: at Horeb 'ye saw no manner of similitude' (Deut 4:15) — God revealed Himself by His word, not by a form, and to manufacture a form is to exchange His glory for a likeness and inevitably to shrink Him. The golden calf proves the commandment's edge: Aaron did not announce a new god but proclaimed 'a feast to the LORD' (Exo 32:5) — Israel was worshiping YHWH by an image, and the LORD counted it apostasy. From this commandment the Reformed churches drew the regulative principle of worship — God is to be worshiped only as He has appointed in His Word — and, with the historic Reformed confessions, declined to make images of God in any person, the Lord Jesus included, since no image can show what He is: 'God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth' (John 4:24). The commandment carries a promise as wide as its threat: mercy unto thousands of them that love Him and keep His commandments.
webster_summary: The Decalogue's second word (Exo 20:4-6): the true God must not be worshiped by images or man-devised means — the golden calf was a 'feast to the LORD' and yet apostasy; the root of the regulative principle of worship.

The root of the regulative principle: God worshiped only as His Word appoints.

corruption_summary: The second commandment is corrupted when it is collapsed into the first (as Rome's numbering does, hiding it), when images are defended as 'aids' to devotion, and when worship is governed by what feels authentic rather than what God has appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: Image-as-aid misreading. The perennial defense — from the calf to the medieval church — is that the image is not the god, only a help to worship Him. The commandment forecloses exactly this: Aaron's calf was offered as a feast TO THE LORD (Exo 32:5), and God judged it as rebellion, because every manufactured likeness lies about the God who showed no similitude and shrinks His glory to the measure of the craftsman. The dictionary holds, with the historic Reformed confessions, that the true God is not to be imaged in any person — and that He has given His own appointed pictures: the Word, the water, the bread and the cup.

Authenticity-worship misreading. The modern form of the corruption rarely carves idols; it enthrones the worshiper, governing worship by what feels moving, expressive, or authentic to the self. But the second commandment locates the rule of worship in God's appointment, not man's invention — the regulative principle: what He has not commanded for His worship, He has forbidden. The dictionary commends the freedom in this: worship by God's appointment is worship He has promised to bless, and the conscience is freed from every device of men.
roots_summary: The Decalogue's second word: no images, no man-devised worship — the manner of worship belongs to God's appointment; root of the regulative principle, proved at the golden calf.
